question: What is a contract-first approach in API development?

options.text: The backend writes code from which the OpenAPI specification is automatically generated
options.explanation: This is the code-first approach. In it, implementation is primary and documentation is secondary — the API design is dictated by code, not intent.

options.text: The specification is agreed upon by the team before implementation begins, and types and mocks are generated from it
options.explanation: Correct. Contract-first: openapi.yaml → frontend generates types and MSW mocks → backend implements. Teams work in parallel.

options.text: Frontend and backend agree on the API in Confluence, without a formal specification
options.explanation: Agreements in Confluence are an informal contract. Contract-first implies a machine-readable specification (OpenAPI) from which code can be generated.

options.text: Development begins only after signing a legal contract with the client
options.explanation: This has nothing to do with API design. Contract-first is a technical term: the OpenAPI specification as a technical contract between teams.

question: Why does openapi-generator require Java, but openapi-typescript does not?

options.text: openapi-generator is written in Java and runs on the JVM, openapi-typescript is on Node.js
options.explanation: Correct. openapi-generator is a Java project running on the JVM. openapi-typescript is written in TypeScript and runs on Node.js, so it requires no additional runtime dependencies.

options.text: openapi-typescript uses WebAssembly instead of Java for speedup
options.explanation: openapi-typescript does not use WebAssembly. It is simply written in TypeScript/Node.js, which makes it native to the npm ecosystem.

options.text: Java is needed for OpenAPI 2.0 support, openapi-typescript only works with OpenAPI 3.x
options.explanation: Java is needed because the tool itself is written in Java, not because of an OpenAPI version. openapi-generator supports both versions.

options.text: openapi-generator can be run without Java via the npm package @openapitools/openapi-generator-cli
options.explanation: Partially true, but this npm package still downloads and runs a Java artifact internally. The Java dependency does not disappear.

question: You use openapi-typescript. Which of the following does it NOT generate?

options.text: TypeScript interfaces for schemas
options.explanation: Incorrect — this is the primary function of openapi-typescript. It generates types for all schemas from components/schemas.

options.text: React Query hooks (useQuery, useMutation)
options.explanation: Correct — openapi-typescript does not generate hooks. For hooks you need orval or a manual wrapper via openapi-fetch.

options.text: MSW mocks for testing
options.explanation: Correct — MSW mock generation is not part of openapi-typescript. This is functionality of orval or separate tools.

options.text: Typed paths and request parameters
options.explanation: Incorrect — this is exactly what openapi-typescript does: generates a paths structure with full types for parameters and responses of each endpoint.

question: How is the OpenAPI construct allOf: [$ref: A, {type: object, properties: {...}}] expressed in TypeScript?

options.text: Union type: A | { ... }
options.explanation: No, union type (|) corresponds to oneOf / anyOf — 'one of the options'. allOf means 'all options at once'.

options.text: Intersection type: A & { ... } or interface extends A
options.explanation: Correct. allOf requires conformance to all schemas simultaneously — this is the analog of intersection type (A & B) or interface extends A in TypeScript.

options.text: Generic type: Array<A>
options.explanation: Array<A> corresponds to type: array + items: $ref A. allOf is about combining structures, not arrays.

options.text: Mapped type: { [K in keyof A]: A[K] }
options.explanation: Mapped types are a TypeScript construct for type transformations. Code generators do not create mapped types from allOf.

question: Your team of 10 people (5 frontend, 3 backend, 2 mobile) uses the same OpenAPI. Which type generation strategy is most suitable?

options.text: Each developer generates locally as needed
options.explanation: With this approach, different developers will have different versions of types. This is a source of elusive bugs: 'it works on my machine, not on yours'.

options.text: openapi-typescript for everyone — it supports all languages
options.explanation: openapi-typescript is only for TypeScript/JavaScript. It won't work for mobile (Swift/Kotlin).

options.text: openapi-generator in CI: different generators for TS, Swift, Kotlin; results published as packages
options.explanation: Correct. openapi-generator supports 50+ languages. CI runs the needed generators when the spec is updated and publishes results — each platform takes its own package.

options.text: orval with multi-language mode for all platforms
options.explanation: orval is focused exclusively on JavaScript/TypeScript. It is not suitable for Swift and Kotlin.
